summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's 2015 Penal Code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries up to seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained after independence and enhanced in the first post-independence penal code adopted in 2015. The UK Foreign Office records same-sex activity as a crime and confirms that no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people.

Exposure is not limited to prosecution. The US State Department's 2023 reporting states that openly LGBTQI+ persons risk imprisonment and for that reason did not participate in the political process, and that societal discrimination against them continues. The same report found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. A 2011 State Department report relayed by Asmarino records societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians, and documents the government labelling disloyal individuals as "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles."

Foreign nationals are not shielded. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, a gay Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government called him a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local laws including Article 600 of the Penal Code. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one described as openly homosexual; the Eritrean ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the provisions of law prohibiting homosexual relations, and Italian diplomats condemned the action.

Detention and abuse are documented. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, known for housing political prisoners and journalists; abuse, torture and beating of prisoners is commonplace. Gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have been subjected to severe abuse, including physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers, on a 2002 UK refugee claimant account that is unconfirmed.

Criminalisation undermines health and care access. ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing it makes prevention programs directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an "area of concern." There are no laws banning conversion therapy, and OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma; LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea and cannot adopt. The government has rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appeal to legalize same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people," with no major efforts to change or rescind existing laws. In 2010 Eritrea, with other African states, rejected the Yogyakarta Principles. State censorship of LGBTQ issues is compounded by heavy social stigma; in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programs detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality.
tangentialFactors:
Eritrea's broader human rights environment compounds the risk faced by LGBTQI+ visitors. The US State Department's 2010 Human Rights Report records torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service alongside criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma. The UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported the death penalty was not used in 2013, though some prisoners have been illegally executed according to the same source inventory.

The UK Foreign Office raised concerns about the absence of anti-discrimination protection for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people bilaterally and through the EU, indicating sustained but so far unsuccessful diplomatic pressure. Eritrea's rejection of the Yogyakarta Principles in 2010 alongside other African states, and its dismissal of the Universal Periodic Review appeal, place it among the jurisdictions formally resisting international norms on sexual orientation and gender identity.

outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military face severe abuse rests on a single 2002 UK refugee claimant account that is unconfirmed; the pattern is not independently corroborated in the inventory.

No youth-specific care findings are recorded for Eritrea in the source inventory. Whether Article 310(1) has been actively enforced against foreign visitors in recent years, as distinct from the documented 2003, 2004 and 2013 cases, is not sourced here. The inventory does not resolve whether the current Penal Code's Article 310(1) replaced or renumbered the earlier Article 600 referenced in the Mannina expulsion, though both are described as the same criminalising provision.
